items.feedback: Right. What makes a system an agent is the loop: the model picks an action, the program runs it, and the result comes back for the next step. A longer prompt or a bigger model changes what one call can do, not the structure.

Right. The model only writes a request that names check_calendar and gives the machine and date as arguments. The program around it runs the tool. This fixes the answer you gave on your first attempt.

You picked 'no change; left to run longer, it will eventually fix the bug'. That is tempting, but the agent is getting the same failing result 40 times, so more steps add nothing. The program needs a stopping condition, such as a step limit, that ends the loop and reports back to a person. Your first attempt picked this, so check how you reasoned about it this time.

Your number, 4, is right: three tool requests plus the final answer. Your reason is not. You wrote that the model 'runs' the tools itself. It only requests them, and the program runs each one. The count works because each model call ends with one request or the final answer. Count 4 as one call for the question plus one for each of the three results.

Right, and you gave both parts: the result goes back in as the next input, and the model uses it to decide its next step. The group-chat comparison works. The model has no other way to learn the result, because it only sees the text it is given.

The name is part of it, but not enough. The model is given a description for each tool: its name, what it does and the parameters it takes. It picks the tool whose description fits the request. Your first attempt said this better. A name alone can mislead, for example a tool called check_calendar that also books. This is why writing good tool descriptions matters for the makerspace assistant.

summary: You have the core of the agent loop down: q1, q2 and q5 are right, and you now see that the model only requests a tool call. Two things to fix. First, the model never runs tools; the program does, and your q4 reasoning still says otherwise. Second, an agent needs a stopping condition, and the model has to rely on full tool descriptions, not just names. Next step: redo q3 and q6 from memory after re-reading the part of the agent-loop lesson on stopping and on tool descriptions, then move on to context and memory.
